front: Visual metaphor: memory management is like a toy shop's parts management. Give the three shared properties and their OS meaning.
back:
• Intelligently sized containers: memory is managed in pages or segments; the size of these containers is an important design consideration
  • Not all parts needed at once: processes do not need all their memory at the same time, so subsets of their state are brought in and out of memory as needed
  • Optimized for high performance: moving state in and out is optimized with hardware support (TLBs, caches) and software algorithms (page replacement, memory allocation)

front: Memory management: which physical resource does the OS manage here, and on whose behalf?
back: The OS manages physical memory (DRAM) on behalf of one or more executing processes.

front: Memory management: what does the OS give a process to decouple it from physical memory, and how are the two related?
back: The OS gives each process an address space of virtual addresses. Almost everything uses virtual addresses, and the OS translates them into physical addresses where the data actually lives.

front: Memory management: how does the size of the virtual address space compare to physical memory?
back: The range of virtual addresses visible to a process can be much larger than the actual amount of physical memory behind the scenes.

front: Memory management has two broad responsibilities. What are they?
back:
• Allocation: track used vs. free memory, and move content between physical memory and secondary storage (disk).
  • Arbitration: quickly translate a virtual address to a physical one and validate that the access is legal.

front: Memory management: why does allocation need to involve secondary storage like disk?
back: Because physical memory is smaller than virtual memory, some virtual locations may not be present in physical memory and reference disk instead. The OS must be able to replace physical memory contents with contents from disk.

text: In page-based memory management, the virtual address space is subdivided into fixed-size {{c1::pages}}, physical memory is divided into {{c2::page frames}} of the same size, and arbitration is done via {{c3::page tables}}.

front: Memory management: how does segmentation differ from paging in its allocation unit and arbitration?
back: Segmentation allocates flexibly-sized segments (not fixed-size pages) that map to regions of physical memory and can be swapped in and out. Arbitration uses segment registers supported by modern hardware.

front: Memory management: which mechanism dominates in modern operating systems, paging or segmentation?
back: Paging is the dominant memory management mechanism used in modern operating systems.

front: Hardware support: what component converts virtual addresses to physical addresses, and where does it live?
back: The memory management unit (MMU), contained in every CPU package. The CPU issues virtual addresses to the MMU, which converts them into physical addresses.

front: Hardware support: what three kinds of problems can the MMU signal with a fault?
back:
• The memory access is illegal (memory not allocated).
  • There are insufficient permissions for the access.
  • The requested page is not present in memory and must be fetched from disk.

front: Hardware support: how do designated registers help memory translation in paging vs. segmentation systems?
back: In a page-based system, registers can point to the currently active page table. In a segmentation system, registers may point to the segment base address, the segment size, and the total number of segments.

front: Hardware support: why does the MMU include a small cache of translations, and what is it called?
back: Because address translation happens on every memory reference, the MMU caches virtual/physical translations in the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) to make translation much faster.

front: Hardware support: the OS maintains page tables, but who performs the actual address translation, and why does that matter?
back: The hardware performs the actual translation. So the hardware dictates which memory management modes are available (page-based or segment-based), what kinds of pages there can be, and the virtual and physical address formats, since it needs to understand both.

front: Hardware support: which memory management aspects are done in software, and which does the lecture focus on?
back: The actual allocation of memory to processes and the replacement policies are done in software and are more flexible; the lecture focuses on these software aspects.

front: Page tables: what is their purpose and what mapping do they provide?
back: Page tables convert virtual memory addresses into physical memory addresses. For each virtual address, an entry maps it to a physical address, so the page table serves as a map from virtual to physical addresses.

front: Page tables: why keep page size equal to page frame size? What does this save?
back: Keeping them equal means the OS only has to translate the first address of a page to the first address of the frame; the rest map to corresponding offsets. This reduces the number of entries needed in the page table.

front: Page tables: a virtual address splits into which two parts, and what is each used for?
back:
• Virtual page number (VPN): the first portion, used as an index into the page table.
  • Offset: the rest of the address, added to the frame's base.

front: Page tables: describe the full translation from a virtual address to a physical address using VPN, PFN, and offset.
back: The VPN indexes the page table to produce the physical frame number (PFN), the first physical address of the frame. The PFN is summed with the offset to produce the actual physical address referencing a specific DRAM location.

front: Page tables: what is allocation on first touch, and why is it used?
back: Physical memory is allocated only when a process first accesses (touches) a virtual region. On first access the OS takes a free physical page and creates a page table entry. This ensures physical memory is allocated only when really needed, since programmers may create data structures they never use.

front: Page tables: what happens to pages a process hasn't used for a long time?
back: They may be reclaimed: their contents are swapped out to disk and no longer present in physical memory, with other content taking the corresponding physical slot.

front: Page tables: what does the valid (present) bit indicate, and what does the MMU do when it is 0?
back: The valid bit is 1 if the page is in memory with a valid mapping, 0 otherwise. If the MMU sees it is 0 on an access, it raises a fault and traps to the OS, which decides whether to permit the access and where to bring the page into DRAM.

front: Page tables: after a swapped-out page is brought back in on access, why is a new mapping established?
back: Because it is unlikely the physical address will land at the exact same PFN + offset as before, so a new page mapping is reestablished once access is granted.

front: Page tables: how many does the OS create, and what must happen on a context switch?
back: The OS creates one page table per process. On a context switch it must swap in the page table of the new process. Hardware helps with a register pointing to the active page table; on x86 this is the CR3 register.

front: Page table entry: what two fields does every entry have at minimum?
back: At least a PFN and a valid bit (also called the present bit, indicating whether the virtual memory contents are present in physical memory).

front: Page table entry: what is the dirty bit, when is it set, and where is it especially useful?
back: The dirty bit is set whenever a page is written to. It is useful in file systems where files are cached in memory: it shows which cached files were written and thus need to be updated on disk.

front: Page table entry: what does the access bit track?
back: Whether the page has been accessed at all, for reads or for writes.

front: Page table entry: what do protection bits specify?
back: Whether a page is allowed to be read, written, or executed.

front: Pentium x86 page table entry: what do the R/W and U/S bits mean?
back:
• R/W: a single permission bit; 0 means reads only, 1 means both reads and writes are permitted
  • U/S: whether the page can be accessed from user mode or only from supervisor (kernel) mode

front: Pentium x86 page table entry: besides Present, Dirty, Accessed, R/W and U/S, what else is in the entry?
back: Flags that control the behavior of the hardware caching subsystem (for instance, whether caching is disabled for the page), and some unused bits. Present, Dirty and Accessed mean the same as in the generic entry.

front: Page table entry: besides translation, what else does the MMU use the entry's bits for?
back: To determine the validity of the access. If the hardware determines the physical access cannot be performed, it causes a page fault.

front: Page fault: what sequence occurs when the hardware cannot perform a physical access?
back: The CPU places an error code on the kernel stack and generates a trap into the OS kernel, which invokes the page fault handler. The handler decides what to do based on the error code and the faulting address.

front: Page fault: what does the error code tell the handler?
back: Information such as whether the page was not present and must be brought in from disk, or whether a permission/protection violation forbade the access.

front: Page fault on x86: how is the error code generated and where is the faulting address stored?
back: The error code is generated from some flags in the page table entry, and the faulting address is stored in the CR2 register.

front: Page table size: what two quantities do you need to compute a page table's size?
back: The size of a page table entry and the number of entries (equal to the number of VPNs in the virtual address space).

front: Page table size (32-bit): what is the entry size, and how large is the addressable memory?
back: Each entry is 4 bytes (32 bits), including PFN and flags. A 32-bit architecture has 2^32 bytes = 4GB of addressable memory.

front: Page table size (32-bit, 4KB pages): work out the number of entries and total table size.
back: Entries = 2^32 / 2^12 = 2^20 entries. At 4 bytes each: 2^20 * 2^2 = 2^22 bytes = 4MB per page table.

front: Page table size (64-bit, 4KB pages, 8-byte entries): what is the computed size?
back: 2^3 * 2^64 / 2^12 = 32PB for a single flat page table.

front: Page table size: are page tables shared or per-process, and why does that make the flat design wasteful?
back: Page tables are a per-process allocation. A flat table assumes an entry for every VPN whether or not the process needs it; since a process does not use all theoretically available virtual memory, this is unnecessarily large.

front: Multi-level page tables: what do the outer and inner levels point to?
back: The outer level, the page table directory, holds pointers to page tables (not to frames). The inner level holds proper page tables whose entries have the PFN and protection bits pointing to page frames in physical memory.

front: Multi-level page tables: what is the key space-saving property regarding holes in the virtual address space?
back: Internal page tables exist only for virtual regions that are actually valid. Any holes in the virtual address space result in no internal page table being allocated.

front: Multi-level page tables: what happens to the page table structure when a process requests more memory via malloc?
back: The OS checks and may create another inner page table for the process, adding a new entry in the page table directory. The new page table corresponds to the newly requested virtual memory region.

front: Multi-level page tables: in a two-level scheme, how is the virtual address split and what does each component index?
back: Into outer index, inner index, and offset. The outer index selects the page table directory entry (a page table); the inner index selects the page table entry (the PFN); the offset indexes into the physical frame.

front: Multi-level page tables worked example: with outer=12 bits, inner=10 bits (p2), offset=10 bits (d), how much memory can one inner page table address?
back: One page table has 2^10 entries, each addressing 2^10 bytes, so each page table addresses 2^10 * 2^10 = 1MB of memory.

front: Multi-level page tables: with a 1MB-per-table granularity, how are large gaps handled? Give the lecture's example.
back: Gaps of 1MB or greater need no page tables. With 2^10-entry inner tables, pages 0-999 fall in table 0 and pages 30000-30999 fall in tables 29 and 30, so the 28 page tables in between (1 through 28) need not be allocated, unlike a flat table which must cover every VPN with no gaps.

front: Multi-level page tables: how can the hierarchy be extended beyond two levels?
back: Add more layers: a third level with pointers to page table directories, a fourth level that is a map of page table directory pointers, and so on.

front: Multi-level page tables: why is deeper hierarchy especially important on 64-bit architectures?
back: 64-bit page table requirements are larger and address spaces are often more sparse, giving larger gaps between allocated tables. With four-level addressing, entire page table directories can be saved from allocation thanks to these gaps.

front: Multi-level page tables: what is the tradeoff of adding more levels (benefit vs. cost)?
back: Benefit: inner tables cover smaller regions, so gaps are more likely to match the granularity and the table shrinks. Cost: more memory accesses per translation (more components to walk), increasing translation latency.

front: Multi-level quiz: a process uses 12-bit addresses, 6-bit offset (64-byte pages), with first 2KB and last 1KB allocated. How many entries does a single-level table need?
back: A single-level table with a 6-bit VPN needs an entry for every virtual page regardless of use: 2^6 = 64 entries.

front: Multi-level quiz: same 12-bit setup with a 2-bit outer and 4-bit inner index. How many total entries, and what is the reduction vs. the flat table?
back: Each outer entry covers 2^(4+6) = 1KB; one of the four outer regions is unallocated and needs no inner table. Each inner table has 2^4 = 16 entries, and three are needed: 3 * 16 = 48 entries, a 25% reduction over the 64-entry flat table.

front: TLB: how many memory references does translation need in a single-level vs. a four-level page table (before counting the TLB)?
back: Single-level: 2 references (one for the page table entry, one for physical memory). Four-level: 4 page table accesses, then 1 access to the data itself (5 total).

front: TLB: what is it, where does it sit, and what happens on a hit vs. a miss?
back: The translation lookaside buffer is a hardware page table cache in the MMU. On each translation the TLB is referenced first; on a hit the full page table walk is bypassed, on a miss the full lookup is still performed.

front: TLB: besides the address translation, what else do TLB entries hold?
back: All the necessary protection and validity bits, so the MMU can generate a fault if the access is not correct.

front: TLB: why can even a small number of cached entries give a high hit rate?
back: Because memory references usually have high temporal and spatial locality.

front: TLB: give the modern x86 per-core TLB sizes mentioned in the lecture.
back: A 64-entry data TLB and a 128-entry instruction TLB per core, plus a shared 512-entry second-level TLB.

front: Inverted page tables: what is the motivation for them over per-process page tables?
back: High-end platforms have physical memory on the order of tens of terabytes, while the virtual memory of an address space can reach petabytes and beyond. A page table structure on the order of the available physical memory is much more efficient than one on the order of the virtual memory, so the inverted table mirrors the physical memory layout: one system-wide table whose entries point to frames.

front: Inverted page tables: how are they managed, and what does each entry point to?
back: They are managed on a system-wide basis (not per-process), and each entry points to a frame in main memory.

front: Inverted page tables: what does a logical memory address contain here?
back: The process id (PID) of the process, the virtual address, and the offset.

front: Inverted page tables: how is a lookup performed and how is the physical address formed?
back: A linear scan of the table is performed; the correct entry is validated by the combination of PID and virtual address. The index of that entry is the physical frame number, which combined with the offset gives the exact physical address.

front: Inverted page tables: why is there no clever search technique to speed up the linear scan?
back: Physical memory can be arbitrarily assigned to different processes, so the table is not really ordered: two consecutive entries may represent memory allocated to two different processes.

front: Inverted page tables: linear scans are slow. What two things speed up lookups?
back: The TLB speeds up repeated lookups, and hashing page tables supplement the design: the address is hashed into a hash table whose entry points to a small linked list of possible matches, limiting the linear search to a few possibilities.

front: Segmentation: how is the address space divided, and into what logically meaningful parts?
back: Into components of arbitrary size (segments) corresponding to logically meaningful sections such as code, heap, data, or stack.

front: Segmentation: what two parts make up a segmented virtual address, and how is translation done?
back: A segment selector and an offset. The selector is used with a descriptor table to obtain the physical (base) address of the segment, which is combined with the offset to produce the linear address of the memory reference.

front: Segmentation: in its pure form, how is a segment represented and defined?
back: As a contiguous section of physical memory, defined by its base address and its limit registers.

front: Segmentation: how are segmentation and paging combined in practice?
back: They are used together: the segmentation process produces a linear address from the logical address, which is then passed to the paging unit to produce the physical address.

front: Segmentation: contrast x86_32 and x86_64 support for segmentation and paging.
back: x86_32 supports segmentation and paging (Linux allows up to 8K segments per process plus 8K global segments). x86_64 keeps segmentation for backward compatibility, but the default mode is to use just paging.

front: Page size: what determines it, and what size results from a 10-bit vs. a 12-bit offset?
back: The number of bits in the offset determines page size. A 10-bit offset gives 2^10 = 1KB; a 12-bit offset gives 2^12 = 4KB.

front: Page size: what is the default Linux x86 page size, and what offsets do large and huge pages need?
back: Default is 4KB. Large pages are 2MB (21-bit offset); huge pages are 1GB (30-bit offset).

front: Page size: what is the benefit of larger pages for the page table and TLB?
back: More offset bits means fewer VPN bits, so fewer pages, a smaller (lower-footprint) page table, and more TLB hits.

front: Page size: by what factor do large pages shrink the page table vs. 4KB, and huge pages vs. large?
back: Large pages reduce the page table size by a factor of 512 relative to a 4KB page; switching from large to huge pages reduces it by another factor of 512.

front: Page size: what is the downside of larger pages, and what is it called?
back: If a large page is not densely populated, there are larger unused gaps within the page itself: wasted memory known as internal fragmentation.

front: Page size: where do large and huge pages make the most sense?
back: In settings like databases or in-memory data stores; otherwise smaller 4KB pages are commonly used.

front: Page size: what page sizes does Solaris 10 on SPARC support?
back: 8KB, 4MB, and 2GB, illustrating that different system/hardware combinations support different sizes.

front: Page table size quiz: 12-bit architecture, single-level page table, 32-byte pages. How many page table entries?
back: A 32-byte page needs a 5-bit offset, leaving 7 bits for the VPN, so the table needs 2^7 = 128 entries.

front: Page table size quiz: 12-bit architecture, single-level page table, 512-byte pages. How many page table entries, and what is the lesson?
back: A 512-byte page needs a 9-bit offset, leaving 3 bits for the VPN, so the table needs only 2^3 = 8 entries. Larger pages mean fewer virtual pages and a smaller page table.

front: Memory allocation: what do kernel level allocators handle?
back: Allocating pages for the kernel and for certain static process state at creation (code, stack, and so forth), and tracking the free memory available in the system.

front: Memory allocation: what do user level allocators handle, and via what interface?
back: Dynamic process state (the heap), dynamically allocated during execution, via malloc and free, which request memory from the kernel's free pages and later release it.

front: Memory allocation: after a malloc, is the kernel still involved in managing that memory?
back: No. Once the kernel allocates memory through a malloc call, it is no longer involved; that memory is under the purview of the user level allocator.

front: Memory allocation: in what terms do user level allocators differ, and which allocators does the lecture focus on?
back: They have different tradeoffs in cache efficiency and in how well they behave in a multithreaded environment. The course does not cover their internals; it focuses on kernel level allocators, whose design principles are also used in some user level allocators.

front: Memory allocation challenges: what is external fragmentation?
back: Multiple interleaved allocate and free operations leave noncontiguous holes of free memory, so requests for large contiguous blocks of memory cannot be satisfied (in the lecture example, even though four frames are free).

front: Memory allocation challenges: in the lecture example, why can a 4-frame request fail even with 4 free frames available?
back:
Setup: 16 page frames, requests for 2 or 4 contiguous frames, currently one 2-frame request and three 4-frame requests, allocated first come, first served.

The frames must be allocated contiguously, and after the earlier 2 frames are freed the free frames are not contiguous, so the allocator cannot satisfy the request.

front: Memory allocation challenges: in the 16-frame example, how does an allocator smarter than first come, first served avoid the failed 4-frame request?
back: Knowing requests are for 2 or 4 contiguous frames, it leaves a gap after the 2-frame allocation and places 4-frame requests at a granularity of four frames. When the first 2 frames are freed, four contiguous frames are free, so the new 4-frame request succeeds.

front: Memory allocation challenges: what must a good allocator do to limit external fragmentation?
back: Lay out and allocate memory so it can coalesce free page frames when memory is no longer in use, keeping free space contiguous.

front: Linux kernel allocators: name the two main ones.
back: The buddy allocator and the slab allocator.

front: Buddy allocator: what does it start with, and how does it satisfy a request?
back: It starts with a free consecutive region whose size is a power of two. On a request it repeatedly subdivides into halves (each a power of two) until it finds a chunk small enough that is still a power of two and can satisfy the request.

front: Buddy allocator: starting from a free 64-unit chunk, trace requests for 8, 8, then 4 units, then the freeing of both 8-unit chunks.
back:
• Request 8: 64 splits into 32 + 32, one 32 into 16 + 16, one 16 into 8 + 8; one 8 is used
  • Request 8: the other 8 from that split is used
  • Request 4: the other 16 splits into 8 + 8, one 8 into 4 + 4; one 4 is used
  • Freeing one 8 leaves some fragmentation; freeing the other 8 lets the two buddies combine into one free 16

front: Buddy allocator: what happens on a free, and how far can it continue?
back: On free, a chunk checks its same-size buddy; if the buddy is also free the two aggregate into a larger chunk. This checking continues up the tree, aggregating as much as possible (e.g. rebuilding all the way from 1 unit back to 64).

front: Buddy allocator: what work does the buddy structure save on a free?
back: Without it, the allocator would potentially have to scan all neighboring pages to determine which are free and how far the free area extends. With it, a chunk only checks its same-size buddy, so the aggregation of free areas is fast.

front: Buddy allocator: why are chunk sizes powers of two?
back: So that the addresses of buddies differ by only one bit (e.g. a 4-unit chunk at address 0b000 has its buddy at 0b100, address 4), which makes buddy computation easier.

front: Buddy allocator: what fragmentation problem does it have, and what example illustrates it?
back: It suffers internal fragmentation because of its power-of-two granularity, which is a problem for the many Linux kernel structures that are not near powers of two in size (e.g. the task struct is 1.7KB).

front: Slab allocator: what does it build, on top of what, and how does it serve allocations?
back: It builds custom object caches on top of slabs (contiguously allocated physical memory). At startup it pre-creates caches for objects (e.g. the task struct or directory entry objects); a request uses a cache element, and if none is free the kernel allocates another slab of contiguous memory.

front: Slab allocator: why does it avoid both internal and external fragmentation?
back: Entries are the exact size of the objects stored, so there is no internal fragmentation; and since only objects of a given size go in a given slab, there are never any un-fillable gaps, so no external fragmentation.

front: Demand paging: what is it, and where do swapped-out pages reside?
back: Allocated pages need not always be in physical memory; a backing frame can be repeatedly saved to and restored from secondary storage. Pages are swapped from DRAM to a special swap partition, which can be on disk, a flash device, or even another node's memory.

front: Demand paging: what is the present bit set to for a swapped-out page, and what happens on reference?
back: Its present bit in the page table entry is set to 0. On reference the MMU raises a page fault exception, trapping into the kernel.

front: Demand paging: outline what the kernel does once it finds a page has been swapped out.
back: It locates the page on the secondary device, issues an I/O to retrieve it, picks a free frame (very likely not the same one as before), updates the page table entry with the new PFN, then returns control to the process.

front: Demand paging: after the page is brought in, how does the faulting instruction complete?
back: Control returns to the process and its program counter is restarted with the same instruction, so the reference is made again and this time succeeds.

front: Demand paging: what does it mean to pin a page?
back: To pin a page is to disable swapping for it, so it stays resident in physical memory and keeps the same physical address instead of being paged out to secondary storage.

front: Page replacement: when does the OS swap pages out of main memory?
back: Periodically, a page out daemon runs when occupied memory exceeds a threshold and CPU usage is low enough that the daemon does not interrupt applications too much.

front: Page replacement: ideally which pages should be swapped out, and why can't we do that directly?
back: Ideally the pages that will not be used in the future, but we cannot know that directly, so we use historic information to make informed predictions.

front: Page replacement: what is the LRU policy, what is its intuition, and which hardware bit does it use?
back: Least-Recently Used (LRU) swaps out the page used least recently, on the intuition that recently used pages are more likely to be needed soon. It uses the access bit to track whether a page has been referenced.

front: Page replacement: besides recency, what other property makes a page a good eviction candidate, and which bit helps?
back: Pages that do not need to be written out to disk, since writing is slow. The dirty bit (maintained by MMU hardware) tracks whether a page has been modified.

front: Page replacement: what must the swapping algorithm do about non-swappable pages?
back: Make sure non-swappable pages (for instance pages containing important kernel state or pages used for I/O operations) are not considered by the currently executing swapping algorithm.

front: Page replacement: what aspects of swapping can be configured in Linux?
back:
• The threshold page count that determines when pages start getting swapped out
  • How many pages are replaced during a given period of time
  • Linux categorizes pages into different types, which helps narrow down the decision of which pages to replace

front: Page replacement: what is Linux's default replacement algorithm, and what does it do?
back: A variation of LRU that gives a second chance: it performs two scans before determining which pages to swap out.

front: LRU quiz: describe the pathological loop where LRU faults on every access.
back: An array of 11 page-sized entries is looped over on a system with only 10 physical pages. After loading pages 1-10, accessing the 11th evicts page 1 (least recently used), the very next page needed; bringing page 1 back evicts page 2, and so on, so 100% of accesses are demand paged. This is why OSes can be configured with different replacement policies.

front: Copy-on-write: what problem does it solve when creating a new process?
back: Copying the parent's entire address space is wasteful because many parent pages are static and will not change, so COW avoids the unnecessary copying cost.

front: Copy-on-write: how is the new address space set up initially, and what protection is applied?
back: The new process's address space (entirely or in part) points to the parent's; the same physical address is referred to by two different virtual addresses. The shared pages are write protected to track accesses.

front: Copy-on-write: what happens on a write to a shared, write-protected page?
back: The MMU detects the write protection and raises a page fault. The OS then creates the copy of the page, updates the faulting process's page table to point to the new physical memory, and only the pages being written are copied.

front: Copy-on-write: why is it named that way, and when is the copy cost paid?
back: It is named copy-on-write because the copy cost is paid only when a write request actually comes in; read-only sharing saves both memory and the CPU cycles of copying.

front: Copy-on-write: after a copy is made, is write protection removed from the original page? On what does it depend?
back: It depends on how many other processes still share it. If other references to the write-protected page remain, it must stay protected so their writes continue to trigger faults.

front: Checkpointing: what is it and what problem does it address?
back: A failure and recovery management technique that periodically saves process state, so after a failure the process can restart from a known recent state instead of being reinitialized.

front: Checkpointing: contrast the simple approach with the hardware-optimized incremental approach.
back: Simple: pause the process and copy its entire state. Optimized: write-protect the state and copy once, then as the running process keeps dirtying pages, use MMU support to track dirty pages and copy only the diffs, giving incremental checkpoints.

front: Checkpointing: what is the downside of incremental checkpoints, and how is it mitigated?
back: Recovery is harder because state must be rebuilt from multiple diffs. This is mitigated by aggregating the diffs in the background to produce more complete checkpoints.

front: Checkpointing: what is rewind-replay in debugging?
back: Rewind restarts execution from an earlier checkpoint; replay re-runs from there to reproduce an error. One can go back to older and older checkpoints until the error is found.

front: Checkpointing: how do the same mechanisms support migration, and how can it be implemented?
back: Migration checkpoints a process to another machine and restarts it there (useful for disaster recovery or consolidation). It can be implemented by repeating checkpoints in a fast loop until so few pages are dirtied that a pause-and-copy becomes acceptable, or unavoidable.

front: Checkpointing quiz: the more frequently you checkpoint, (a) the more state you checkpoint, (b) the higher the overheads, (c) the faster you recover from a fault, (d) all of the above. Which?
back: (d) all of the above.

front: Checkpointing quiz: what is the frequency tradeoff?
back: More frequent checkpointing means faster recovery (less execution to replay) but higher overhead and more state captured. Spacing checkpoints out lets repeated writes to a page amortize into a single dirtied page; you gain faster recovery at the cost of higher overhead.
